newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China Light sees low but steady growth.
newsitem.headline: China Light sees low but steady growth.

text.p: China Light & Power Co Ltd on Monday forecast low, single-digit growth in the next few years and said profits to be derived from added electricty demand in Hong Kong would only surface in the longer-term.
"We are forecasting 3.5 percent to 5.0 percent growth in local unit sales till the end of the decade," chief executive and managing director Ross Sayers said at a news conference.
The company announced a 14.8 percent decline in earnings to HK$4.84 billion for the year ended September 30, 1996 on Monday, a touch lower from a 13 percent decline forecast by analysts.
The decline was partly due to a large exceptional gain of HK$1.28 billion in the previous financial year from sale of its Hok Yun site. The company reported no exceptional gains in 1996.
China Light is building a residential complex on the Hok Yun site with Cheung Kong Holdings Ltd. The first phase of 740 units is scheduled for completion in April 1997.
Sayers would not forecast future income from this project.
On its core business of electricity generation, the company said it would face slower growth rates in unit sales than previously forecast.
"We are going through a difficult period for a few years," said chairman Sidney Gordon.
This was because of a more rapid-than-expected decline in demand from the manufacturing sector and the general economic slowdown in Hong Kong in the mid-1990s, officials said.
Full commissioning of its natural gas-fired Black Point power plant has also been deferred due to over-capacity.
"Four units of Black Point which were originally scheduled to be commissioned in 1998-99 have been rescheduled for 1998-2001," Sayers said.
"Our reserve capacity is 50 percent of output, whereas 35 percent to 40 percent would be sufficient for a Hong Kong company," Gordon said.
"Export sales to China amounted to 520 million units, a 70 percent decline over the previous year," the company said in a statement.
The company appeared to be making little progress in negotiations on power plant projects in China and India.
There, however, appears to be one bright spot in the company's earnings outlook.

"The majority of the large-scale infrastructure and urban development projects in Hong Kong are occurring in our supply area," said Sayers, adding that these could help raise long term demand for electricity.

Hong Kong has a host of huge infrastructural projects such as the Chek Lap Kok airport, new railway lines and related property development plans which are forecast to boost electricity demand in coming years.
